item.title: How to Use n8n Workflows as MCP Tools in Claude Code
item.description:
Introduction

Claude Code writes great code, but your n8n workflows already encode the automations that matter: the newsletter pipeline, the CRM sync, the deploy checks. n8n’s built-in, instance-level MCP server turns those workflows into tools Claude Code can search, inspect, and execute. This tutorial covers enabling the server, connecting Claude Code with OAuth or an API key, exposing your first workflow, and running it from the terminal, on n8n Cloud and self-hosted instances alike.

item.title: How to Migrate n8n from npm to Docker Before n8n 3.0
item.description:
Introduction

If you run n8n from npx n8n or a global npm install n8n -g, your installation has an expiry date. n8n 3.0, scheduled for October 2026, drops support for npm-based installs entirely, and the n8n package on npm stops at the last 2.x release. This guide migrates a working npm install to Docker Compose without losing workflows, credentials, or execution history. It is written for self-hosters on a VPS or home server who installed n8n the quick way years ago and now need the supported path. If you followed our Ubuntu VPS install guide, the backup habits from that post apply here too.

item.title: n8n 3.0 Upgrade Guide: The Breaking Changes Checklist Before You Update
item.description:
Introduction

n8n 3.0, scheduled for October 2026, is the most disruptive release in the project’s recent history. It ends npm and npx installs for self-hosters, removes more than 35 legacy nodes and helpers, retires Chat Hub, and tightens security defaults that change how Code nodes, community packages, and webhooks behave. This guide is the pre-upgrade checklist for anyone running a production 2.x instance, on Docker or npm, who owns workflows that must keep working the morning after the upgrade. If you have not yet moved off npm, read our npm to Docker migration guide alongside this one, because that move is now mandatory.

item.title: Meta WhatsApp Business MCP Server Setup: Let an AI Agent Onboard Your Business Number
item.description:
Introduction

Setting up WhatsApp Business messaging used to mean four open tabs: the Meta Developer Console, Business Manager, the API reference, and your code editor. On September 15, 2026, Meta shipped the WhatsApp Business Tools MCP server, which hands that entire sequence to an AI agent. This tutorial shows you how to connect the server to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, or ChatGPT, authenticate with OAuth, and onboard a phone number, create templates, and configure webhooks by describing what you want in chat.

item.title: How to Fix n8n CVE-2026-44791: Patch the XML Node Prototype Pollution Bypass
item.description:
Introduction

If you self-host n8n, there is a critical patch you need to apply. In May 2026, n8n published security advisory GHSA-wrwr-h859-xh2r for CVE-2026-44791, an XML node prototype pollution bypass rated CVSS 4.0 9.4 Critical. An authenticated user with permission to create or modify workflows can dodge the earlier XML node fix and, combined with other nodes, reach remote code execution on the n8n host. This guide walks you through checking whether your instance is vulnerable, applying the emergency workaround, upgrading on Docker and npm, locking down permissions, and verifying the fix. It is written for anyone who runs their own n8n, from a single Docker container on a VPS to a multi-worker queue mode cluster. If you installed n8n with our Ubuntu VPS install guide, start at Step 1.

item.title: How to Use Ollama with n8n AI Agent: Run Local LLMs That Actually Call Tools
item.description:
Introduction

Running your n8n AI Agent on a cloud LLM means every run costs tokens and every prompt leaves your network. Ollama removes both problems: it serves open models on your own machine, and n8n talks to it over plain HTTP with no API key. This tutorial walks you through the full setup, from pulling a tool-capable model to fixing the one problem that breaks most Ollama agents, which is the model answering in prose and silently skipping your tools. It is written for n8n 2.40 and later, self-hosted, and assumes you already have a working n8n instance.

item.title: Make.com MCP Server Tutorial: Turn Your Scenarios into AI Tools
item.description:
Introduction

Your Make scenarios already automate the boring parts of your business. This tutorial shows you how to expose those scenarios as tools that an AI agent can call directly from Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor. By the end, you will have connected the Make MCP server, published a scenario as a callable tool with a well-designed input schema, locked the agent down to exactly the scenarios it needs, and handled the timeout behavior that trips up most first-time setups. It is written for Make users who already build scenarios and now want agents to run them.

item.title: MCP Postgres Server Tutorial: Safe Read-Only Database Access for AI Agents (2026)
item.description:
Introduction

Letting an AI agent touch your database is the fastest way to make it useful and the fastest way to lose data. One hallucinated UPDATE without a WHERE clause is all it takes. This tutorial shows the setup that earns both: an AI assistant that can explore schemas, run analytical queries, and explain slow query plans against PostgreSQL, while two independent layers stop it from writing anything. You will install the actively maintained Postgres MCP Pro server, create a least-privilege read-only database role, and lock the server into restricted mode. It is written for developers who already know what an MCP server is; if you do not, start with our Model Context Protocol pillar guide first.

item.title: MCP Stateless Spec Migration Guide: Move Your Server to 2026-07-28 Without Downtime
item.description:
Introduction

If you run an MCP server built on the 2025-era Streamable HTTP transport, your request lifecycle starts with an initialize handshake and depends on a sticky Mcp-Session-Id header for everything that follows. On 28 July 2026 the Model Context Protocol shipped revision 2026-07-28, which deletes both of those concepts and makes every request self-describing. MCP co-creator David Soria Parra calls it “[MCP’s] most important [release] since remote MCP first launched.” This guide migrates your server to the new stateless wire: what to delete, what to implement (server/discover, per-request _meta, the new headers), how to keep 2025-era clients working during the transition, and how to regression-test the whole thing. It is written for developers who already operate an MCP server over Streamable HTTP. If you have never built one, start with our Model Context Protocol pillar guide first.

item.title: n8n Agents Tutorial: Build a Telegram AI Agent from Scratch (2026)
item.description:
Introduction

On September 25, 2026, n8n launched Agents, a building block that lives next to your workflows instead of inside them. If you have wired a Chat Trigger to an AI Agent node and wished the result had its own identity, history, channels, and schedules, this is it. You will build a personal Telegram assistant: an OpenRouter model, Todoist and Gmail tools, a reusable skill, a daily schedule, and a workflow that calls the agent back. Facts come from n8n’s official docs and video walkthrough; node parameters and the self-hosted setup were verified against n8n 2.41.4 in our lab.

item.title: n8n Queue Mode Scaling Tutorial: Run Worker Processes with Redis (2026)
item.description:
Introduction

This tutorial is for self-hosters whose n8n instance has started to groan: webhook calls timing out, scheduled runs piling up behind each other, the editor freezing while a big execution churns. You will convert a standard single-process n8n install into a queue-mode cluster: one main instance that receives triggers, a Redis-backed job queue, and a pool of worker processes that run executions in parallel, all wired together with Docker Compose.

item.title: How to Build an AI Support Chatbot in n8n: RAG Knowledge Base, Memory, and Human Escalation
item.description:
Introduction

Support teams answer the same questions every day: password resets, pricing plans, refund policies, setup steps. A rule-based FAQ bot deflects only the questions you anticipated, and every unexpected phrasing lands back in the human queue. This tutorial builds the next level in n8n: an AI support chatbot that searches your real support documents for each question, remembers the conversation, and escalates to a human with a summary when it genuinely cannot help. Every node name and parameter default below was verified against n8n 2.41.4’s own node definitions on a lab install.

item.title: n8n Chatbot with Memory Tutorial: Build a Bot That Remembers Conversations
item.description:
Introduction

A chatbot without memory answers every message as if it were the first. Users repeat themselves, the bot contradicts itself, and the experience feels broken. This tutorial fixes that in n8n: you will wire a Chat Trigger to an AI Agent node, attach the Simple Memory sub-node, and end up with a chatbot that remembers names, preferences, and context across messages. Every node name, parameter default, and option below was verified against n8n 2.41.4’s own node definitions on a lab install, so what you read is what you will see in the editor.

item.title: n8n Code Node JavaScript Tutorial: Run Modes, $input, Data Transforms & Debugging
item.description:
Introduction

Every n8n user hits the same wall: the no-code nodes cover 80 percent of the work, and the remaining 20 percent is a data transformation that would need a Rube Goldberg chain of Set, Filter, and Merge nodes. That is exactly what the Code node is for. It is the escape hatch that keeps you inside n8n instead of reaching for an external script, and it is the skill that separates n8n beginners from n8n builders.

item.title: n8n Postgres Tutorial: Connect, Query, and Automate (2026)
item.description:
Introduction

Sooner or later every serious n8n workflow outgrows in-memory data. You want orders stored where a crash cannot lose them, a customer table your whole team can query, or an audit log that survives a workflow rewrite. PostgreSQL is the natural home for that data, and n8n ships a first-class Postgres node for talking to it. This tutorial walks you from an empty database to a working workflow that creates tables, inserts rows, reads them back, updates them, and runs parameterized queries safely. It is written for automation builders who know their way around an n8n canvas but have never wired it to a real database, and every step was verified against n8n 2.40.7 and the node’s published parameter names.

item.title: How to Build an MCP Server in Python (2026): Tools, Resources, and Claude Desktop Setup
item.description:
Introduction

Building an MCP server in Python is the fastest way to give an AI assistant access to your own data and actions: your notes, your database, your internal APIs. The official Python SDK does almost all the protocol work for you. You write small, type-hinted Python functions, and the SDK turns them into tools with JSON schemas, validates every call, and speaks the Model Context Protocol to any host. This tutorial walks through the current SDK (v2, which supports the 2026-07-28 MCP specification) from an empty folder to a working server connected to Claude Desktop, with testing and the five mistakes everyone makes.

item.title: n8n Vector Store Tutorial: Store and Retrieve Embeddings with Pinecone and Qdrant
item.description:
Introduction

A vector store is the memory layer of a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline: you convert documents into embeddings, long lists of numbers that capture meaning, store them in a vector database, and at query time pull back only the chunks relevant to the question. This tutorial wires that whole loop into n8n: ingest documents into Pinecone or Qdrant with the Vector Store node, then let an n8n AI agent retrieve your own documents as a tool. Every node name, mode, and parameter below was verified against n8n 2.40.7’s own node definitions, cross-checked with Pinecone’s official n8n skill published by Pinecone’s developer relations team.

item.title: n8n AI Agent Tutorial: Build Your First AI Agent with Tools and Memory
item.description:
Introduction

The n8n AI Agent node turns a language model into something that can do things: look up information, calculate, call APIs, and remember earlier conversation, all inside a visual workflow. This tutorial builds a working research-assistant agent step by step, using a real n8n 2.40.7 install I ran locally to verify every node name, option, and requirement below.

Quick answer

Add an AI Agent node to a workflow, connect three things to it, a chat model (e.g. OpenAI), at least one tool (e.g. Calculator, Wikipedia), and optionally memory (Window Buffer Memory), then write a System Message describing the agent’s job. The agent reasons in a loop, calls tools as needed, and returns a final answer. You must connect at least one tool, or the node won’t run.

item.title: Claude Code MCP Setup: Connect Any MCP Server in Minutes
item.description:
Introduction

Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-native coding agent, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how you plug it into everything outside the terminal: issue trackers, databases, design tools, monitoring dashboards. This tutorial sets up MCP servers in Claude Code from scratch, picking the right scope, writing the exact CLI commands, and verifying the connection. Every command below was run against a real Claude Code 2.1.283 install on 2026-09-28, and the transcripts are the actual output.

item.title: MCP Server Tutorial: Build Your First MCP Server from Scratch
item.description:
Introduction

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets AI assistants use external tools, read your files, query your database, call your APIs. In this tutorial you’ll build a real, working MCP server from scratch with the official TypeScript SDK, watch the actual protocol messages flow between client and server, and connect it to Claude Desktop. Everything below was tested hands-on; the protocol traces are copied from a live run.

item.title: n8n Error Handling Tutorial: Retries, Error Outputs & Error Workflows
item.description:
Introduction

You build a workflow that syncs orders from an API into a spreadsheet. It runs fine for three weeks, then the API has a bad night, and you find out from a customer, because the failure happened silently.

n8n’s default on node failure is blunt: stop the entire workflow and mark the execution failed. Fine while building, but production automations, anything running on a schedule or webhook while you sleep, need a failure plan. Here are its three layers, smallest to largest:
